Ten questions. They are medium difficulty on purpose — answerable if you understood
the model, not answerable by skimming for keywords. Every one has a wrong answer that sounds right,
because those are the misconceptions worth catching.

Answers and per-option feedback are collapsed. Commit to an answer before you expand it.

> The [interactive version](../08-quiz.html) scores you as you go and gives feedback on the option
> you actually picked.

### Question 1

The `seller` brand overrides `radius.md` (a **global** token) from `8px` to `2px`. It does not mention `button.radius` at all. Why does the button's corner radius change anyway?

A. Because `button.radius` aliases `radius.control`, which aliases `radius.md` — and the brand block re-declares that whole chain in scope.
B. Because girih recalculates every dependent value at build time and writes the final `2px` into the brand block.
C. Because `BrandProvider` reads the brand at runtime and passes the resolved radius down through React context.
D. Because component-tier tokens automatically inherit from same-named global tokens.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Exactly. The override is two hops down, and it arrives because the alias chain is re-declared inside `[data-brand="seller"]`, so the whole chain recomputes there.

**B** — ❌ · This is the approach girih deliberately avoids. Flattening to literals would freeze the values and break nested brand scopes. The emitted CSS keeps `var()` references live.

**C** — ❌ · BrandProvider only sets a `data-brand` attribute. It resolves no values — all the resolution is CSS, in the browser.

**D** — ❌ · There is no automatic inheritance by name. The connection is the explicit `{alias}` reference in the token files.

</details>

### Question 2

The `seller` brand overrides exactly 3 tokens, but its emitted CSS block contains 12 declarations. What are the other 9, and what breaks if you omit them?

```css
[data-brand="seller"] {
  --ds-radius-md: 2px;
  --ds-color-primary: var(--ds-color-green-600);
  --ds-color-primary-hover: var(--ds-color-green-700);
  --ds-radius-control: var(--ds-radius-md);
  --ds-button-radius: var(--ds-radius-control);
  /* …7 more… */
}
```

A. Every token that transitively references an overridden one. Without them, a two-hop chain declared only in `:root` resolves against `:root` and ignores the brand scope.
B. Fallback values, in case the brand block loads before the `:root` block.
C. Duplicates emitted for specificity, so the brand block outranks `:root`.
D. Every token in the design system, re-declared for isolation.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct — that is the dependents closure. And note the failure mode: direct references appear to work while multi-hop ones silently do not, which is the most misleading kind of bug.

**B** — ❌ · Custom properties are resolved at use time, not parse time, so declaration order between blocks does not matter here.

**C** — ❌ · An attribute selector already outranks `:root`. Specificity is not the problem being solved.

**D** — ❌ · That would be 109 declarations, not 12. Only the closure of the overridden paths is re-emitted.

</details>

### Question 3

A brand overlay adds a token path that does not exist in the base token set. What does girih do, and why is that the right call?

A. Hard error. If brands could add tokens, a contract could reference something one brand has and another lacks — so "one component set for every brand" would stop being true.
B. Merges it in and emits it only inside that brand's scope.
C. Warns, and drops the token from the output.
D. Adds it to the base set for all brands, with a null value elsewhere.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Right. This is the override-only rule, and `validateBrandParity()` exists to enforce the same invariant from the other direction.

**B** — ❌ · That is what a naive deep-merge would do, and it is precisely the fork-by-accident girih is built to prevent.

**C** — ❌ · A warning would let a broken mental model persist. girih makes it an error.

**D** — ❌ · This would silently mutate the shared base from inside a brand overlay — the opposite of the intended direction of control.

</details>

### Question 4

`.ds/ir/*.json` and `.ds/manifest.json` are generated by girih and also committed to git, while `packages/design-system/` is generated and gitignored. What distinguishes them?

A. Both committed files are inputs to future runs or to review: the IR is the reviewable contract diff, and the manifest is the drift baseline that must survive a fresh clone.
B. They are small enough to commit without bloating the repository.
C. They are written by the CLI rather than by a generator package.
D. They are hand-editable, unlike the React output.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Exactly. The rule is not "generated files are not committed" — it is "generated files are not edited". Those are different claims.

**B** — ❌ · Size is not the criterion. The React output is not enormous either; it is excluded because nothing needs it in git.

**C** — ❌ · Which package writes a file has no bearing on whether it belongs in git.

**D** — ❌ · The opposite — the manifest is machine-managed and editing it disables drift detection. `GIRIH1011` fires if it is corrupt.

</details>

### Question 5

`validateSpecs(irs, build.graphs, TEMPLATE_REGISTRY)` receives the token graphs for _every_ brand rather than just the default. What defect does that plural catch?

A. A token reference that resolves under the default brand but not under another one — which would otherwise pass locally and fail in production for one brand.
B. Two brands resolving the same token to different values.
C. A brand with no overrides at all.
D. Contracts that reference tokens from more than one tier.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct, and it is the most common real defect in this area. The diagnostic is prefixed with the brand name so you know which one is missing the token.

**B** — ❌ · That is not a defect — it is the entire point of a brand. Different values, identical structure.

**C** — ❌ · Perfectly legal. The `marketplace` brand in the example overrides nothing and its overlay file is `{}`.

**D** — ❌ · Also legal and normal — the Button contract references component, semantic and global tokens.

</details>

### Question 6

A teammate edits `packages/design-system/src/button.tsx` directly to add a class, then runs `girih generate react`. What happens, and what should they do?

A. It refuses and names the file. The right move is `girih eject Button`, which carries their hand edits into a tracked fork rather than discarding them.
B. It overwrites the file, since generated output is always authoritative.
C. It merges the hand edits with the freshly generated output.
D. It succeeds but marks the file stale in the manifest for later review.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct. `--force` would work but discards exactly the work the gate is protecting. Ejection is the gate's own remedy, and it preserves the edits.

**B** — ❌ · That would silently destroy their work, which is the failure mode `.ds/manifest.json` exists to prevent.

**C** — ❌ · girih does not attempt a merge here. A three-way merge exists only as a planned feature for ejected forks.

**D** — ❌ · There is no "stale but proceed" state. Drift is a stop condition.

</details>

### Question 7

You remove one value from a variant axis — `size: ['sm', 'md', 'lg']` becomes `['sm', 'md']` — and run `girih bake`. What version bump is proposed?

A. Major. Anything removed is breaking, because some consumer's `size="lg"` call site is now invalid.
B. Minor, since the component still exists and most usages still compile.
C. Patch, because only the emitted CSS and the type union changed.
D. Whatever you pass via `--bump`.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct, and note that nobody had to remember this: the bump is derived from the contract diff by `diffSignatures()`, not chosen by a human.

**B** — ❌ · Minor is for additive changes. A removal invalidates existing call sites regardless of how many.

**C** — ❌ · Patch is for token value changes — different pixels, same API. This changes the API.

**D** — ❌ · There is no such flag. Removing the human judgement from versioning is the design goal.

</details>

### Question 8

In the live demo, switching brands changes the Button and Badge but leaves `PaymentButton` looking identical. Is that a bug?

A. No — it is an extension that pins its colours to `{color.text}` and `{color.background}`, which no brand overrides. It is deliberately brand-independent.
B. Yes — extensions do not receive brand-scoped custom properties.
C. Yes — extensions must be re-generated per brand and this one was not.
D. No — extensions are always excluded from brand theming by design.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Right. A checkout call-to-action that should look the same everywhere. It is an intended property of the extension, not a gap in the mechanism.

**B** — ❌ · They do. The extension's CSS uses `var()` like everything else; it simply references tokens this brand does not override.

**C** — ❌ · Nothing is generated per brand. One component set, one stylesheet, values swapped by scope.

**D** — ❌ · Too strong. An extension referencing `{color.primary}` would rebrand normally. This one just does not.

</details>

### Question 9

Two tokens named `color.primary.hover` and `color.primary-hover` both exist. What does girih do?

A. Fails with `GIRIH3003` — both collapse to `--ds-color-primary-hover`, which would be a silent last-one-wins in CSS.
B. Emits both; CSS custom property names are case- and separator-sensitive so they stay distinct.
C. Renames the second one automatically with a numeric suffix.
D. Warns, and keeps whichever came last in file order.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct. The name transform joins segments with hyphens and lowercases, so distinct paths can collide. Making it a hard error turns an afternoon of debugging into a build message.

**B** — ❌ · After the transform they are byte-identical. There is nothing left to distinguish them.

**C** — ❌ · Silent renaming would make the emitted variable name unpredictable from the token path, breaking the `TokenPath` contract.

**D** — ❌ · That is exactly the silent last-one-wins behaviour the check exists to prevent.

</details>

### Question 10

Why do `generate`, `build` and `bake` all route through a single `composeReact()` function instead of each computing its own file list?

A. So they can never disagree about what the package contains — otherwise `bake` could ship a file set nobody reviewed.
B. To avoid running the token pipeline three times, for performance.
C. Because the emitted file list is needed to compute the publish signature.
D. To keep the CLI file under a line-count limit.

<details>
<summary><b>Show answer and feedback</b></summary>

**Answer: A**

**A** — ✅ correct · Correct. It makes a whole class of bug unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely, which is why you extend that function rather than the three call sites.

**B** — ❌ · A real benefit, but not the reason. Correctness is: three independent implementations could drift apart.

**C** — ❌ · True — the signature does include the file set — but that is a consequence of sharing the function, not the motivation for it.

**D** — ❌ · No such constraint exists, and `cli.ts` is comfortably the largest file in the repository anyway.

</details>
